info.name: Mountain Breath API
info.description:
Living API contract for the Mountain Breath backend.

**Rule (docs/RULES.md):** every commit that adds, changes, or removes a route must update this collection in the same commit — request, variables, and tests.

**Usage:** start the API (`go run ./cmd/api` in `backend/`), then send requests here, or use the Collection Runner to execute the whole suite as a smoke test. Postman's cookie jar carries the session cookie between requests automatically.

**Admin folder:** set the collection variables `adminEmail` / `adminPassword` to a local admin account first (register a user, then promote it: `UPDATE users SET role='admin' WHERE email='...';` via psql). Values are not committed — they are your local secrets.

Folders mirror the roadmap phases from docs/PROJECT_PLAN.md.

Every public page in every language, generated by the API because only it knows the product slugs (the static routes are listed in the handler; journal POSTS are absent — their slugs live in frontend markdown, a recorded cost of decision #77). item.description: Session-cookie auth. The cookie (mb_session, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax) is set by register/login and carried automatically by Postman's cookie jar. Run these top-to-bottom.

request.description: Creates a customer account and starts a session. The pre-request script generates a unique email per run.
Returns the logged-in user, resolved from the session cookie. 401 without a valid session.

Wrong password and unknown email return the SAME error — the API must not reveal which accounts exist (user enumeration).

E8: the login body also accepts "remember": true — the session and its cookie then live 30 days instead of 7. The token is rotated at every login either way. Login is rate limited per (IP, email): 10 attempts per 10 minutes, counted BEFORE the password check so guessing cannot even spend the shop's bcrypt time. The 11th answers 429 too_many_attempts.
Deletes the session server-side and expires the cookie.
The session is gone server-side — the old cookie (if any survived) is worthless.

item.name: Products in drams — a different number, not a conversion

request.description:
The same catalogue priced for the Armenian market. The dram figures come from variant_prices rows the shop set by hand, so they are NOT the dollar price times a rate — which is the whole reason for per-market pricing: a shelf price is a business decision, and a rate would move the price tag between two page loads.

Note the minor units change scale as well as value: 1400 is $14.00 (two decimals) while 6700 is 6,700 ֏ (a dram has no subdivision). Any client dividing by 100 is wrong here by two orders of magnitude.

The 150 g pouch of propolis crumbs is seeded WITHOUT a dram shelf price, deliberately — it is the one variant that exercises the fallback. Its AMD figure is the USD price converted at the newest fx_rates row and snapped to the currency's rounding_step (10 drams), so it lands on 22,620 rather than a round number like its neighbours.

A currency with neither a shelf price nor a rate produces no price at all: the storefront then shows one line instead of two, and checkout refuses with 409 price_unavailable rather than charging zero.

item.description:
Every price in the design is shown in two currencies, and an order is charged in exactly one of them.

The model: a price is not a property of a product, it is a property of a (product, market) pair. `variant_prices` holds one row per pair; `fx_rates` is only the FALLBACK for a market the shop has not priced by hand, plus the record that keeps an old order reportable. Totals are summed independently in each market and never converted, because rounding a sum is not the sum of roundings.

(Compare E4, where a non-purchaser reviewing a PUBLIC product rightly gets 403 — the resource there is public and only the action is denied.)

THE test of the phase's security design: the client never sends money. The request shape has no money field, and DisallowUnknownFields turns a body that tries into a 400 before any handler code runs — the total is not ignored, the request is refused.

item.name: Missing address fields come back at once (400)

request.description: Every gap in ONE response, keyed by the JSON path the form posts (`address.postal_code`) so the React form attaches each message to its input — the same convention as `variants[0].sku` since Phase 6.

The design's own words made a rule: "Cash — on delivery, AMD only". A courier collecting dollars in Yerevan is not a thing, so the domain rejects the pairing as a field error the client can FIX (switch currency, or pick another method). E5 made the rule expressible by giving every order a currency.

item.description:
Screen 05: a checkout that collects an address and produces an itemised order.

The model in one paragraph: the client sends CHOICES (address, payment method, note); the server computes every figure — subtotal from locked shelf prices, shipping from per-currency rate rows (base waived over the free threshold, the cold-chain surcharge never), VAT contained in the subtotal per "Prices include VAT", and a CHECK constraint holding subtotal + shipping − discount = total on every row, forever. The address is snapshotted onto the order exactly as prices are: an order is a closed record, and nothing the customer later edits may reach into it.

item.name: Promotions & hive club (Phase E7)
item.description:
The promo box, the free-shipping bar and the member discount — all priced by ONE pure calculator (domain.Price) that the preview, the cart page and order creation share.

The hive club is not a stored tier: the design's sign-in screen defines it as having an account, so both perks (first delivery free, 8% off after the first order) derive from a count of the user's non-cancelled orders.

Run these signed in (Register/Login first) with something in the cart (Set cart item).

POST with no body: everything it prices is server-side state (the cart, the applied code, the customer's order history) plus the negotiated language/currency. The order that POST /orders later creates is priced by the same function with the same inputs read under lock — which is what makes 'cart, checkout and the order agree to the dram' a property of the design.

item.name: Account settings (A5)
item.description:
Canvas 10's write paths: profile (name + phone, echoed back as the fresh user), the signed-in password change (verifies the CURRENT password, then revokes every session except the caller's own — contrast the reset flow's revoke-all), and the notifications panel's two real channels (decision log #87): the order-updates flag on users, and the harvest-notes toggle read from the newsletter table (ON goes through the newsletter's own double-opt-in POST /newsletter/subscribe; OFF is DELETE /account/newsletter, tokenless because the session proves email ownership).

Run signed in.

request.description: Both fields, whole-value semantics; both optional (empty is an answer, only excess is refused). Email is deliberately NOT here — changing the account's identity is a verification-shaped problem, not a form field. Responds with the fresh user (same shape as /auth/me) so the client sets its cache from the response.

204 on success; every session except THIS one is revoked. A wrong current password is a FIELD error (`current_password: incorrect_password`), not a 401 — the session is fine, one input is not. An OAuth-born account (empty hash) fails the same way and sets its first password through the reset flow, which verifies the inbox instead.

request.description: The two REAL channels in one read: `order_updates` (the users column F2's mailer will honour) and `newsletter` (none | pending | subscribed, derived from the newsletter table by the account's email). The canvas's other toggles have no machinery and no endpoint — deliberately.
The one persisted toggle. Defaults TRUE for every account.
The harvest-notes toggle's OFF. Tokenless: the session proves email ownership; the emailed token remains the anonymous path. Idempotent — 204 even with nothing to unsubscribe.

item.name: Accounts (E8)
item.description:
Wishlist, password reset, the address book and Google sign-in.

The reset flow reuses the sessions pattern a third time: the email carries a raw 256-bit token, the table stores its SHA-256, single use is enforced under a row lock, and consuming a token revokes every session. The wishlist is set-semantics like the cart. The address book is the account page's CRUD behind the checkout's prefill.

Run the wishlist/address requests signed in (Register/Login first).

request.description: Requests a reset link. The answer is 204 WHETHER OR NOT the email exists — login already answers identically for unknown email and wrong password, and a reset endpoint that said 'sent!' for members and 'no such account' for strangers would be a free membership oracle. Rate limited per (IP, email) like login. The mailed link lands in the requester's language (?lang= / cookie / Accept-Language, as everywhere).

exec: pm.test("status is 204 — for members and strangers alike", () => {

request.description: Spends an emailed token. Unknown, already-spent and expired tokens all answer the same 400 invalid_token — one answer for every kind of no, so a token-guesser has nothing to calibrate against. A valid token sets the new bcrypt hash and DELETES every session the user has: a reset means 'someone may have my credentials', and a reset that leaves a stolen session alive changed the lock while leaving a window open.

item.name: Add an address to the book

request.description: The account page's book behind the checkout prefill. The FIRST entry becomes the default whatever the flag says (a book with entries but no default would leave the prefill nothing to stand on); a later entry claiming the default demotes the old one inside one transaction, because the one-default-per-user partial unique index rejects the intermediate state. Validation uses the checkout's exact field keys (address.street …). A4 adds `leave_with_neighbour` — a fact about the PLACE that prefills the checkout checkbox; each order still snapshots its own copy.
Defaults first. Every row is scoped to the session's user in the WHERE clause — someone else's address id behaves exactly like no address (the 404-not-403 rule, applied to a book).
Cleanup for re-runs. Deleting the default is allowed and leaves the book without one — a true statement about the customer's choices; the next checkout simply has nothing to prefill.

Leg 1 of the authorization-code flow: a 302 to Google carrying a random state (CSRF proof, mirrored in a short-lived cookie). 404 when MB_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID/SECRET are unset — unconfigured means the feature does not exist, and the login page's button explains itself. The callback is browser-driven and cannot be usefully exercised from Postman; its tests live in backend/internal/api/account_test.go against a fake Google.

item.name: Newsletter (E9)
item.description:
Double opt-in: typing an address proves nothing (anyone can type anyone's), so the row is created unconfirmed and only the emailed link's click makes it live. The token is the sessions pattern's fourth use with one twist: it is NOT single-use and does NOT expire — it is the subscriber's permanent capability (confirm today, the unsubscribe link at the foot of every future issue).

Confirm and unsubscribe are POSTs from the emailed link's PAGE, a deliberate departure from the plan's GET: corporate mail scanners prefetch every GET link in incoming mail, and a mutating GET gets 'clicked' by a robot before the human opens the message — auto-confirming the very consent double opt-in exists to prove. Scanners follow GETs; they do not submit forms.

request.description: The footer form. 204 whatever the address's history (never seen, pending, already live) — no membership oracle. An already-confirmed subscriber gets NO mail, or every form submit would re-spam the shop's most loyal readers. Rate limited per (IP, email) like login: this endpoint mails arbitrary addresses on request, which unthrottled is a spam cannon. The lang matters — the confirm link lands the reader back in their language.
The one validation: net/mail's RFC grammar (shared with registration via domain.ValidEmail), refused as a field error before any row exists.

The real token arrives only by mail (raw in the message, SHA-256 in the table). Confirming is IDEMPOTENT — people re-click links from their inbox, and 'already confirmed' rendered as an error would read as failure to someone who did everything right. Only an invented token fails.
The same permanent capability pointed the other way, equally idempotent. A real unsubscribe link must keep working forever — it is the one link in any newsletter that must never break.
